articleTitle: Configuring the Parameters of a RVSS to Start a High Torque Induction Motor Load with a Soft Pull-In
abstract: This paper describes the approach to configuring the parameters and overall philosophy of controlling a reduced-voltage soft-starter (RVSS) for a high-torque induction motor load. As long as the induction motor's blocked rotor, breakaway, and pull-up torque are adequate for the torque-speed curve, an RVSS can be controlled and programmed to adjust its thyristor firing patterns to bring the motor up-to-speed and transition it to a bypass running state. The other necessary concern would be whether utility Sag at the PCC would be acceptable when the programmed current limit of the RVSS is at its threshold. Otherwise, an adjustable frequency drive (AFD) may be of interest in replace of the full-voltage across-the-line start or RVSS start to better the torque-per-amp ratio and sag at the point of common coupling (PCC).

articleTitle: Reaching Environmental, Social & Governance (ESG) goals with Medium Voltage (MV) Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs)
abstract: Energy consumption and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{CO}_{2}$</tex> emissions, whether through primary sources such as natural gas, coal, oil, or secondary sources such as electric power, are a significant percentage of the variable cost make-up and environmental footprint of cement plant operations. In a market where energy conservation, reducing carbon emissions, and the laser focus on ESG initiatives are gaining C-level attention, it pays to make every dollar spent on procuring that energy worthwhile. Medium voltage variable speed drives (VFDs) are commonly applied on large services such as preheater ID, main bag filter, finish mill, cooler vent, and kiln ID fans. First, VFDs provide the necessary speed and flow control based on process requirements and enable energy savings by exploiting the affinity fan or pump laws. Second, by creatively installing VFDs that eliminate the need for cooling or heating of the built environment is another source of energy and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{CO}_{2}$</tex> emissions savings. Finally, a large part of the cement plant's electric power consumption is in the form of fixed speed induction motors spread across the various “shops”. Motors being a lagging load drag down the overall plant power factor and ultimately lead to higher electric bills and losses in the grid supply. This paper shows the simple math around the above-mentioned areas through which a medium voltage VFD captures value and plays straight into sustainable energy savings, electric cost reduction, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\boldsymbol{CO}_{2}$</tex> emission reductions. The goal of the paper is for prospective industrial power engineers, operators, and financial stakeholders to open new lines of economic and commercial thinking around creatively applying MV drives to not just pumps and fans, but also in other plant applications. The risks of not thinking about large VFDs as a strategic piece of equipment to reduce carbon emissions and electrical costs in an environment of climate change pressures have become too large to ignore.

articleTitle: New Pleated Filters for Cement Kiln Baghouses and Other High-Temperature Applications
abstract: Cement plants today are pressed to operate above design capacity while being subjected to ever-tightening air emission restrictions as a result of environmental regulations. This means that the demands on air pollution control equipment connected to the cement kiln are greater than ever before. Pleated filters have been in use in industrial applications for more than 20 years. They offer several benefits over traditional filter bags and cages such as ease of both installation and removal, reduced air-to-cloth ratio, lower operating differential pressure, and in some cases longer filter life. Until now, there have been many design challenges in creating a pleated filter that can operate continuously at 500°F (260°C) for use in cement kiln baghouses. This paper will introduce you to a new high-temperature pleated filter design. In addition, this new 500°F (260°C) rated pleated filter design is shown to achieve enhanced compartmental flow distribution results when operated at favored lower operating differential pressures when installed and used together with traditional long bags in the same baghouse. This paper will show the novel application of a dual pleated bag filter configuration operated at 500°F (260°C) under high can velocity using advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling.

articleTitle: VFDs on Process Fans - When Are They a Good or a Bad Idea?
abstract: Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) are an established technology on process fans that can save power by utilizing the Fan Laws. VFDs can be a more effective control device for controlling flow on a fan than an inlet damper when utilized correctly. This is especially evident in the case of low voltage motors and/or fans that are operating at a low damper position. This paper will explore various projects at a cement plant in Kansas that have had varying degrees of success. In one case, the VFD worked beautifully and had a very low payback period. In another case, process conditions changed over time and all of a sudden, the power savings from installing VFDs were negligible. This paper will look at how to identify good cases for installing VFDs and how to properly estimate the payback of a VFD project. It will also look at other considerations that need to be made when selecting a VFD, including installation, electrical and automation issues.

articleTitle: Virtual Reliability Manager - How to Become the SMART Cement Plant of Tomorrow Today
abstract: Remote Monitoring Platforms automatically deliver critical real-time data to Cement personnel around the globe with cloud connected controls and sensors. This paper reviews IoT technology for use in the Cement Industry to: • Maximize efficiency – aligns with goals of increased automation • Decrease energy consumption and operating costs through optimization • Assure Health, Safety, and Environmental compliance through awareness and mitigation • Provide ‘virtual’ equipment health checks Four Case Studies review five findings of interest: i. Reduction—unplanned outages ii. Insight—mechanical failures predicted before occurrence iii. Simplification—Ease of access to information iv. Optimization—Eliminate unwanted movement from maintenance work old v. Accuracy & Efficiency—Error-free record keeping Cloud-based control systems remotely monitor not only dust collector conditions, but universally monitor emissions, airflow, vibration, humidity, high temperature or any other data set, from anywhere on most any equipment around the globe. This increases the use of predictive maintenance.

articleTitle: Safety and Maintenance Design Considerations at Terminals
abstract: Bulk material terminal design requires a breadth of disciplines and depth of experience that makes this a unique and challenging field. In the complexity of facility design and layout, designers may overlook important aspects related to safety and maintenance or treat them as secondary concerns. For the long-term profitability and longevity of a facility, however, these may be among the most critical design features. A difficult-to-maintain facility will not be upkept as well as it should be. This can lead to premature failures of equipment, increased operations and maintenance costs, dissatisfied owner/operator, and potential safety hazards. Additionally, unique product characteristics, local climate, or operating conditions can pose less obvious yet serious safety hazards. Unsafe working conditions can result in citations, fines, downtime, and injury or death. Corrections for these hazards may require costly and/or lengthy facility modifications that far exceed the cost or time required to install them initially. This paper is not intended to be an exhaustive review of all safety and maintenance aspects of bulk material terminals. Various points will be discussed to highlight key safety and maintenance features for consideration.

articleTitle: Reducing Compressed Air Consumption for Filter Bag Cleaning with Advanced Cleaning Controls and Cleaning System Design
abstract: The regeneration of filter media in dust collection systems is an important element in the reliability of process equipment, but excess compressed air pressure causes premature filter bag failure in addition to unnecessary electrical consumption. Improvements in pulse-jet technology have enabled the use of filter bags beyond 16 feet which help reduce capital costs of new baghouses. The inherent issue with regenerating the filter media at long bag lengths is the capacity and operation of the pulse valve against the process flow. By utilizing an advanced cleaning controller in a segmented baghouse design, cement producers can extend filter media life and lower compressed air consumption. Offline cleaning requires lower compressed air pressure to regenerate the filter media while gently cleaning the filter bags, therefore reducing operating costs and extending filter media life without the dramatic airflow swings of compartment isolation.

articleTitle: Decarbonization Through Oxy-Combustion and H2 as A Fuel
abstract: Many countries have committed, as per Paris Agreement earlier and reindorsed during COP26, for zero CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> emission within next thirty to forty years, i.e., by 2050–2060. All efforts made so far within cement industry to reduce CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> emissions from AFR (alternative fuel and raw materials) would lower CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> emissions by about 30%. The use of calcined clay (by turning natural clay soils into synthetic pozzolanic materials) may lead to another 40% reductions in CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> emissions by replacing up to 40% clinker in the cement mix. However, further efforts with new technologies are required to meet the future expectations of the cement plants which may need to run on non-fossil fuels with CCUS (Carbon Capture Usage/Storage) capabilities. R&D exercises have already been started to prepare existing and/or future cement plants with net zero ‘Carbon’ emissions. The main technical challenges relate to the effective use of several thermal inputs from a matrix of energy resources, including H2, plasma, microwave, biomass and oxygen/ CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> enrichment through recycling of combustion products. The oxygen enrichment, which substitutes the entire air ‘nitrogen’ in the combustion/cooling air, and the minimization of air-in-leakage - so that a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> enrichment in excess of 95% is assured. This requires minor modifications to almost all the components of a cement plant, including the clinker cooler, kiln and kiln burner, calciner and cyclones, is necessitated. The most critical issue is the inhibition of the calcination rate consequent of the enriched calciner CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. Some results are presented from such R&D efforts, prior to full-scale demonstration, to test the use of non-fossil fuel-based cement production, which can be integrated into a CCUS system as these systems are also being developed at present. The by-product of hydrogen generation (i.e., via electrolysis) will be oxygen that will be essential in replacing N<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> from the oxidant via oxy-combustion, which has shown to enhance combustion and increase clinker production at a number of cement plants. The plant safety and operational issues for adapting these approaches are of paramount importance and needs to be considered carefully.

articleTitle: Small Volume Concrete Walled Silo Solutions
abstract: Traditionally, small volume storage silos (less than 3,000 tons) have been constructed of steel plate. This has become so routine that many owners do not consider a concrete walled silo option. Cost is the major factor regarding this trend in cement storage. While many consider a concrete walled storage silo a better, more permanent structure, economics have caused these decision makers to assume that a steel walled bin is the only real option. However, improvements in design and construction methods have made concrete walled silos more competitive. Additionally, concrete walled silos can routinely be constructed more quickly than a steel walled bin. Design, lead times, fabrication, delivery, and installation of steel bins typically takes months. Advancements in design and construction of concrete walled silos lends to reducing the time for completion considerably when comparing total duration of time from order to commissioning of a silo. It will be shown that a concrete walled silo is not just competitive in cost with steel walled bins of similar storage capacity, but can actually be less expensive than comparably sized steel bins. This is the case regardless of foundation requirements, be it founded on sound bedrock, or relatively low capacity bearing strata. This paper will discuss some key aspects of differences between steel bins and concrete walled silos. Costs, schedule, longevity will all be considered. The paper will discuss generic details of both and draw comparisons of the two options.

articleTitle: Trouble Shooting During Commissioning Phase - A Case Study
abstract: A newly build 100% natural gas fired cement plant, upon commissioning, was facing unusual kiln instability and clinker quality issues. Several concurrent investigations were carried out to identify the cause of the problem and bring plant to the target production rate and clinker quality. The scope of the analysis has been to examine the preheater performance and clinkerization characteristics within the kiln for the operating conditions of 6000 tpd clinker production as per the design configuration. The plant is a 5-stage in-line pre-calciner/kiln design operating with two production lines with specifications corresponding to 3.13GJ/t of clinker; It was demonstrated in a previous publication [1], on firing natural gas or when switching from coal/oil to natural gas (NG) in a cement plant, that the heat transfer characteristics of the lower thermal emissivity natural gas adversely affect the heat transfer within thermal radiative region of the kiln - unless better flame conditions are achieved within the near burner region. For natural gas flame to effectively transfer heat to the bed, it is important to produce a flame of optimum shape and length through the diffusion of the secondary air. Initially, a natural gas flame produces a higher flame temperature regime due to better mixing with the oxygen than coal or oil, however, its heat dissipation rate is much slower leading to lower heat transfer to the bed. In the preheater, of Line 2, hotmeal had uneven LOI from four meal inlets, resulting from the flow stratification. In addition, higher gas temperatures were also observed near the tower region. In the kiln, two burner configurations were tested and compared and alterations to the burners were identified. A combination of improvements to the combustion and raw-meal mixed enabled the plant to meet its target values. Some of the most important results from the study are discussed in the paper.

articleTitle: New Kiln Inlet Gas Analysis Technology
abstract: This paper outlines a new patented gas analysis design for the kiln inlet of a cement plant. The paper will explain why gas sampling is facing more process challenges, particularly from the increased use of alternative fuels in the industry. The paper will describe a how a new patented technology makes it possible to increase the cleaning power of a kiln inlet probe system by combining the force of proven air blasters with cutting edge 3D metal printing nozzle design. The system has been tested in normal plant operations and the customer process objectives and observations from the test are given. The conclusion outlines the importance of having a powerful kiln inlet gas analysis system in order to safely optimize the cement kilns operations.

articleTitle: The Evolution of the Modern Coal Grinding System
abstract: The modern indirect coal grinding system can operate with either hot gases from the kiln hood/cooler or from the discharge of the preheater tower. The firing circuit has been optimized to use a minimum amount of primary air for combustion and thereby utilizing the maximum amount of secondary air from the clinker cooler. This was not the case 50 years ago, when the direct fired system was used extensively as the system of choice. The system had some short comings that came to light as a result of the energy crisis in the early 1970's. This paper will follow the direct fired system to the present-day coal grinding system.

articleTitle: Flexibility with a Modular Grinding Plant - Case Study
abstract: In contrast to the trend towards larger grinding plants, recent years have also shown a shift towards smaller and compact grinding units. Various reasons are for the benefit of smaller production units, depending on local market conditions. The modular grinding system is suited to produce all types of cement independent on feed properties. Incorporated in a modular grinding plant the installation can be transported and erected very fast and efficiently due to the design. Modules are containerized in standard container sizes and delivered pre-assembled. This study will review the selection criteria and rationale behind a plant's decision to install a modular grinding system. The experiences from different modular plants already in operation prove that the erection and commissioning can be accomplished in a very short time, the performance can easily be met by utilizing state-of-the-art vertical roller mill technology.

articleTitle: Use of Battery Energy Storage Systems for Cement Production Facilities
abstract: The increasing priority of decarbonization and corporate ESG (environmental, social, and governance) performance create a unique opportunity for the cement industry to utilize renewable energy and energy storage to lower operating costs, fight climate change, improve resiliency and drive corporate sustainability initiatives. The continued reduction in costs of battery energy storage systems (BESS) now makes onsite battery solutions an effective way to reduce facilities' electricity costs while also reducing their carbon footprint. A BESS can shave peak demand charges and provide energy arbitrage by charging during low-cost periods of the day when renewables are plentiful. When paired with solar PV, industrial-scale batteries can utilize Federal Investment Tax Credits (ITC) to further reduce costs. Deploying onsite battery solutions may also allow the early retirement of increasingly more difficult to operate diesel gen-sets. These systems can provide seven-figure annual savings to a large cement manufacturing plant in the context of “The Battery Decade” and a U.S. energy storage market projected to grow to more than $100 billion over the next 10 years.

articleTitle: The Advancement of Industrial LED Lighting and Its Future Applications
abstract: This paper will discuss key factors to consider in designing an industrial lighting space. Key lighting technologies used in industrial facilities with special focus on light emitting diode (LED) is discussed and compared. This paper will discuss in detail attributes that needs to be considered in selecting a luminaire with emphasis on LED technology. How these attributes impact safety, sustainability, light pollution, and digitalization is discussed. A framework to consider when selecting luminaire is presented as a conclusion.

articleTitle: The (In)direct Electrification of the Cement Industry: The Contribution of Waste Heat Recovery Projects
abstract: This paper is a continuation of previously written and presented ones on the general topic of the direct and indirect electrification of the cement plant operations as part of their pathway toward decarbonation. • Microgrid for Cement Plants - based on IEEE PCA 2019 St Louis - May 2019 •Microgrid for Cement Plants, the Hydrogen parameter - IEEE PCA 2021 virtual- May 2021 It reflects the rapid changes the industry is undergoing under the Energy Transition and Industrial Decarbonation movements. Trends that are fast moving, first the rise of the renewable electricity generation mostly photovoltaic and wind, then the lithium-ion batteries for energy storage, and more recently all matters around hydrogen generation from water electrolysis and oxygen enrichment. Others are still in development, not only on a technological point of view but from their practical applications: flow (or redox) batteries and thermal energy storage (for long duration holding and discharging), CO2 capture, CO2 methanation,… This paper presents one growing solution, that check all the marks, although represent only a small option of the overall pathways toward a decarbonated cement industry. With all the talks around the “new hydrogen economy” and CO2 capture/utilization/sequestration, one could lose sight of the fact that what will allow the decarbonation of the economy is primarily decarbonized and mostly renewable electricity. Electricity produced from waste heat streams is fully decarbonated, fully renewable, and supplied 24/7 (as long as the plant is in operation).

articleTitle: A New Era, The Advent of The PGNA Air Slide Conveyor Analyzer
abstract: In this paper, we detail the development and deployment of a raw meal/finished-cement analyzer based on prompt gamma neutron activation (PGNA) technology in a historical context, followed by lessons learned, system performance discussion, and results from two installations.

articleTitle: Activating Clay to Help Achieve CO2 Emissions Goals by 2050
abstract: The use of supplementary cementitious material in the manufacturing of green cement has been growing in popularity due to the associated environmental and economic benefits. Cement producers and their equipment suppliers are evaluating the different methods, opportunities, and challenges of producing green cement, aligned with a global trend toward net-zero CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> emissions. In this paper the authors discuss in detail the clay activation process, which is a heat treatment of aluminosilicates that promotes the de-hydroxylation of the material resulting in the collapse and breakdown of the clay structure to form compounds with hydraulic binding characteristics. Alternatives for calcined clay production using Rotary Kilns and Flash Calciners are also discussed, including Pros and Cons of both solutions, considering capital expenditure and operating expenses in different scenarios and operational conditions as well as the quality of the final product for each method.
